actions.justification: MANDATORY per SSC Hour-1 Bundle: Measure serum lactate immediately to stratify sepsis severity. If lactate ≥ 4 mmol/L, 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus is required. Serial lactate guides resuscitation.
MANDATORY per SSC Hour-1 Bundle: Blood cultures must be obtained BEFORE antibiotic administration to identify causative organism and guide definitive therapy.
MANDATORY per SSC Hour-1 Bundle: Administer empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour of sepsis recognition, immediately after blood cultures are drawn. Delay increases mortality.

Patient presents with fever, productive cough, and shortness of breath — pulmonary source is likely. Identifying the infection source guides targeted antibiotic selection and source control per SSC guidelines.
Evaluating for organ dysfunction (via SOFA criteria) is essential to confirm sepsis severity, guide resuscitation intensity, and identify any end-organ damage requiring immediate intervention.
CBC will provide WBC count to assess infection severity, hemoglobin for oxygen-carrying capacity (SpO2 94%), and platelet count to screen for early DIC or thrombocytopenia associated with sepsis.
Serial vital sign monitoring is essential in sepsis to track hemodynamic stability, identify deterioration, and guide resuscitation decisions per SSC guidelines.
Patient presents with fever, productive cough, and shortness of breath — chest X-ray is critical to identify pulmonary infection source (pneumonia) and guide antibiotic selection.
Basic metabolic panel evaluates renal function, electrolytes, and glucose — key components of organ dysfunction assessment in sepsis per SSC guidelines.

Patient has lactate of 2.5 mmol/L (>2 mmol/L) and is 45 minutes into the encounter. Per SSC Hour-1 Bundle guidelines, 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid should be administered for hypotension or elevated lactate. Although MAP is currently 88, lactate is elevated and fluid resuscitation is indicated to optimize perfusion.
Initial lactate is 2.5 mmol/L (>2 mmol/L), which per SSC guidelines requires serial lactate measurements to guide resuscitation and assess response to therapy.
After initiating fluid resuscitation, perfusion status should be reassessed to evaluate response to treatment and determine if vasopressors are needed to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg.

Coagulation studies (PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen) are important in sepsis to assess for disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) and organ dysfunction, which is part of the sepsis workup per SSC guidelines.
Procalcitonin is a useful biomarker for bacterial infection severity in sepsis, aids in guiding antibiotic therapy duration, and provides prognostic information per SSC guidelines.

Arterial line placement provides continuous, accurate blood pressure monitoring and facilitates serial blood gas sampling given elevated lactate (2.5 mmol/L) and potential for hemodynamic deterioration in sepsis.

Central venous access is recommended for ongoing resuscitation monitoring, vasopressor administration if MAP drops below 65 mmHg, and CVP monitoring. Placing this proactively while the patient is relatively stable is prudent given elevated lactate and sepsis diagnosis.

Lactate is 2.5 mmol/L (elevated) and the patient may benefit from additional fluid resuscitation beyond the initial 30 mL/kg bolus to support perfusion and guide lactate clearance, while MAP remains adequate.

Patient has lactate of 2.5 mmol/L (elevated >2), SpO2 94%, and MAP of 88 which is currently adequate but fluids have been given. Per SSC guidelines, norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor to maintain MAP >=65 mmHg if hypotension persists during or after fluid resuscitation. Starting vasopressor support is appropriate given ongoing sepsis with elevated lactate and potential for hemodynamic deterioration.

Patient is on norepinephrine (already started) but vasopressin can be added as a second-line vasopressor per SSC guidelines to achieve MAP ≥65 mmHg and potentially reduce norepinephrine requirements. This is the only remaining available action and is clinically appropriate as an adjunct vasopressor in septic shock management.

Patient requires ICU-level care given ongoing sepsis with vasopressor dependence, elevated lactate (2.5 mmol/L), and hemodynamic instability. SSC guidelines recommend ICU admission for septic shock patients on vasopressors.
